turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. What has you in with me today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah thanks. The traffic on the Malahide road was desperate, I was nearly late. It's the ankles, they're swelled up something awful, and I'm forever in the toilet.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the ankles first, in your own words.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Both of them, right up over the sock line. I noticed it, umm, three weeks ago. My neighbour says it's the heat, but sure it's October, what heat.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Three weeks, right. Are they sore at all, or is it mostly the swelling?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Not sore, no. Just puffy and tight, the shoes won't go on. I had to wear the old slip-ons in.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And would you say the swelling stays the whole day?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Depends if I've been mooching about the shops.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. And the passing water, what's that been like?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm up twice a night at least, and during the day I'm in and out. I blame the tea, I drink a fierce amount, six mugs easy. My sister says I'm a teapot with legs.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain when you pass water, or any blood?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain and no blood. It's just often, that's all.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. What tablets are you on at the minute?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The amlodopine, ten milligrams, once a day, for the blood pressure. And the water tablet, uh, frusimide, forty milligrams in the morning. I've been on the blood pressure tablets for years.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Frusemide forty, every morning. Are you getting that one in every morning?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok, we'll leave that as not certain so. And the readings at home, have you been checking them?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I've the little machine from the chemist. This morning it said 128 over 76. Most days it's around one thirty over eighty. My grandson set the cuff up, he's great with phones, he put an app on it I never open.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's handy to have. Let me take it here. There we are, today in the clinic it's 162 over 94, and the pulse is 74.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): 162? God almighty. It was grand at home this morning. I had a coffee on the bus, maybe that did it, and some fella's shopping bag was on my foot the whole way in.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Different places can give you different numbers, you're not imagining it. Can I have a look at the ankles?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Fire ahead. The right one is the fatter, I think. Or maybe they're the same, I can't see past the belly half the time.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Both ankles are pitting, soft swelling up as far as the lower shin. I'm not hearing anything odd in the chest either.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah that's a relief. I was watching some thing on the telly about hearts and I had myself buried, so I did.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain or tightness with all this?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. Breathing is grand too, if you're wondering. I walked from the bus stop no bother.

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. I think the swollen ankles are down to the amlodipine, that tablet is well known for it. The pressure is still high in here, so I'd stop the amlodipine and start you on ramipril, two and a half milligrams once a day.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril, right so. Will I get that from the chemist on the corner? They were out of the other yoke last month and I had to traipse all the way into town.

[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll send the script over and you can collect the ramipril today. The nurse takes your bloods Thursday morning, a kidney test and a fasting sugar, so we know where we are with the new tablet. Nothing to eat from midnight, and hold the morning tablets till after.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday morning, fasting, grand. I'll get the early bus so. Do I still take the water tablet that morning or leave it?

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold all the morning tablets until the bloods are done, the frusemide as well. If the kidney test or the sugar is borderline we'll do a urine protein. If the ankle swelling hasn't settled we'll organise a scan of the legs. I'll see you back here in two weeks anyway.

spec.situation: Patient on amlodipine and a water tablet with swollen ankles and passing urine often; blood pressure read at clinic and at home with different numbers; doctor changes one medicine.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

bad.reason: Dose and morning timing supported, but current use/adherence is uncertain.
bad.text: frusimide (generic_name=furosemide, dose=40 mg, frequency=in the morning, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Home blood pressure readings were reported as 128/76 that morning and usually around 130/80 on most days.
The patient volunteered no breathing problems/shortness of breath and said breathing was 'grand' and they walked from the bus stop without difficulty.
Swelling was described as not painful but puffy/tight, making shoes not fit and requiring old slip-ons.
The swelling was said to vary depending on activity ('depends if I've been mooching about the shops') rather than clearly staying all day.
